### Where the atelier comes from

Loris Malaguzzi put an atelier and an atelierista, a person trained in the arts, into every Reggio Emilia school in the 1960s, and his poem No way. The hundred is there gave the practice its name. Children have a hundred languages, and art is one way of thinking among them. Vea Vecchi, atelierista at the Diana school from 1970 to 2000, wrote the fullest account in Art and Creativity in Reggio Emilia (2010). She describes the atelier as a place of research where materials, light, sound and the body are all ways of knowing, and she argues that the aesthetic sense, the pleasure of a form that fits, is what connects a child's ideas to each other (aesthetics as the activator of learning). Her atelier spread into every class as a mini atelier, which is the model ours follows.

Ann Pelo, in The Language of Art (2007, second edition 2017), carried the atelier into American programs. Her studio practice offers one medium at a time and lets children learn its grammar through weeks of exploration before asking it to carry an idea, and her chapters on paint, clay, wire and collage are the shape of our studio competencies. Lois Lord, who taught art at Bank Street College for decades, built the practice of sorting found materials into trays by color, shape and kind so that children could look before choosing, and Cathy Weisman Topal, who studied with her, carried it into Beautiful Stuff (1999, with Lella Gandini). The Idea bank cards Studio and class ateliers and Art shed hold the set-ups.

### How drawing grows

Rhoda Kellogg collected around a million drawings by young children and in 1969 sorted what she saw. Twenty basic scribbles come first, such as dots, single lines, zigzags and loops. Around three, scribbles close into shapes (diagrams) such as circles, crosses and squares, which children then combine. Around four, mandalas, suns and radials appear, and from them the first people, a circle with lines for legs. Her sequence is a useful map of what to look for, and later researchers, including Claire Golomb, found that the order is less fixed than she claimed and that children skip steps.

Viktor Lowenfeld, in Creative and Mental Growth (1947), named stages by what the child intends. Disordered scribbling comes first, then controlled scribbling once the child sees that the hand makes the line, then named scribbling, when a child tells you what the marks are, often after making them. From about four comes the preschematic stage, where a child draws a person or a house on purpose, and the drawing changes each time. His ages are rough and his stages are still the ones most educators use.

- **Twos and threes.** Scribbles of every kind, big arm movement, pleasure in the mark and in watching it appear. Naming comes after making.
- **Threes and fours.** Closed shapes, combined shapes and the first suns and people. A story told while drawing, and marks named as they are made.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Drawings planned before the pencil moves, with people, animals and places. Details return and grow across drawings of the same thing, and a drawing can be a plan for building or a map of the yard.

Graphic Languages treats every one of these as thinking made visible, and the Idea bank cards Charcoal, Oil pastel and Ink and pens hold the tools for each band in Ways it can grow.

### What the research says about talking to artists

Alfie Kohn's reading of the praise studies, in his article on five reasons to stop saying good job, taken up in The Language of Learning module, is that evaluation turns a child toward the adult's verdict and away from the work. The same research found that description and questions about process keep children working longer and taking more chances. Our Effective Responses list comes from that work, and Vecchi adds one more. Children's work deserves a long look before any words at all.

### Designing the atelier

### What the hands are learning

Cathy Weisman Topal, who taught art to young children at Smith College, wrote in 1983 that hands are the first and most sensitive tools a child brings to clay, and that a child who is handed a tool too soon stops using them. Our practice of a whole block with no tools comes from that idea. Ann Pelo, in The Language of Art (2007, second edition 2017), describes a studio where a child learns the language of a medium the way they learn a spoken one, first by exploring what it can do, then by using it to say something. She keeps one material in front of children for weeks so the exploring has time to turn into speaking.

The body science underneath is plain. Squeezing, pounding and wedging clay send steady pressure through the joints and muscles of the hands and arms (heavy work, or proprioceptive input), which for many children settles attention. Pinching and rolling work the small muscles that later hold a pencil (fine motor strength and the fingertip grasp). Pulling a wire through a block asks both hands to work together with different jobs (bilateral coordination). Beyond Discipline carries the senses in more depth, and the Idea bank card Clay lists what the material feeds and supports, with set-ups for a child who seeks more and one who finds it too much.

### How clay work grows

Claire Golomb watched young children model in clay in 1974 and found that their forms follow a path much like drawing. Handling comes first, then simple shapes, then shapes that stand for something, and children often make a recognizable figure in clay sooner than adults expect when the request is their own. Viktor Lowenfeld described the same movement from scribbling to naming to planning in two dimensions, and clay follows it with its own timing. Age bands are a guide to watching, never a schedule.

- **Twos and threes.** Hands only. Poking, patting, slapping, tearing and squeezing, and finding what water does. A piece may be named after it is made, and the name may change. Clay goes toward mouths as a question, and an educator offers it again for hands.
- **Threes and fours.** Balls, coils and flat pieces appear on purpose. Marks from fists, elbows and the first natural tools. A form gets a name while it is being made, and a child may want to keep a piece.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** A form is planned before the clay is touched, sometimes in a drawing first. Pieces join, stand and hold things, and children solve the problems of balance and hollowing. Work returns over days, and a group piece grows on one board.

The Idea bank card Clay holds the set-ups for each band in Ways it can grow, and A block of clay at arrival holds the first encounter on a hard morning.

### Clay in the Reggio schools

Clay has a place in every atelier in Reggio Emilia, and the schools treat it as a language children return to across years. Vea Vecchi, atelierista at the Diana school for thirty years, describes children turning to clay when an idea is too round, too heavy or too hidden for drawing to hold, such as the inside of a body or the weight of an animal. Topal and Lella Gandini's Beautiful Stuff (1999) grew from a school in Massachusetts where children and families gathered found materials, sorted them and built with them, and its practice of offering a material slowly, with time to sort and look, is the same one we bring to clay. The Reggio educators also keep clay small in quantity and often, so that revisiting is possible. Our block stays out for weeks for the same reason, so that a thread can form.

### The first encounter

### Why a small group, and why the same one

Loris Malaguzzi, in his interview with Lella Gandini in The Hundred Languages of Children, said that small groups of two to five children are the most favorable way for learning to happen, because in a group that size children can argue, borrow each other's ideas and find out that a friend sees the same thing differently. Lev Vygotsky gave that observation its theory in work published in English in 1978 as Mind in Society. What a child can do with a more capable partner today, and alone tomorrow, is the zone of proximal development, and the partner can be an adult or another child. Jerome Bruner and colleagues named the adult's part scaffolding in 1976, the support offered in just the amount needed and withdrawn as the child takes over. Our educator who sets an intention, asks one open question and then waits is scaffolding.

Barbara Rogoff, in Apprenticeship in Thinking (1990), watched children learn in families and communities around the world and found that most learning happens through guided participation, taking part in something that matters alongside people who know how, with the adult adjusting what the child is handed. A small group feeding the goats, planting the bed or building the clay village is guided participation. It is also why the group stays the same for six weeks. Rogoff's apprentices learn from people who know them.

### What group learning looks like

Harvard's Project Zero worked with the Reggio schools for several years and in 2001 published Making Learning Visible. Mara Krechevsky and Ben Mardell set out four features of a learning group. The group includes adults and children. Documenting the process makes learning visible and changes what is learned next. Members are engaged in feeling and in beauty as well as in thinking. And the group builds knowledge that belongs to all of them, beyond what any one child learned. Our binder, our This week in pictures and our drawings posted at eye level are that documentation, and the group's thread is the shared knowledge.

Lilian Katz and Sylvia Chard, in Engaging Children's Minds (1989, third edition 2014), described the project approach, an investigation of a topic from children's own world carried through three phases. Children begin by sharing what they already know and wonder, then investigate through field visits, experts, drawing and building, then conclude by sharing what they found. Katz and Chard are clear that projects suit small groups and that the topic should be close enough to touch. Our collect, meeting time, investigation order is that cycle on a daily scale, and our threads are its first phase.

### How working together grows

Mildred Parten described in 1932 how children's play with others changes with age, and later researchers have found her order loose, with children moving among kinds of play in one morning. It still helps an educator see a group.

- **Twos and threes.** Side by side with the same material (parallel play), with glances, copying and short exchanges. A thread here is often one material the group returns to. Meeting time is brief and sits close to the work.
- **Threes and fours.** Sharing materials and talking about the same thing without one plan (associative play). Children begin to hold a question across days, and the first group drawings and maps appear.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** A shared goal with roles (cooperative play), plans drawn before building, and disagreements the group can work through. Threads become projects, and children can revisit their own documentation and say what to do next.

The Idea bank cards Clipboards everywhere and A clipboard walk hold ways to carry drawing into every sitting, and Studio and class ateliers holds the shared work surface where a group piece grows.

### What the research says about early writing

Marie Clay, a New Zealand researcher, looked closely at what five-year-olds wrote in 1975 and published What Did I Write? She found that children work out the principles of writing on their own before anyone teaches them. A child repeats one shape across a page (the recurring principle), finds that a few marks can be turned and combined into many (the generating principle), lists every letter they know (the inventory principle), and moves marks left to right and down the page (the directional principle). A child also learns that marks carry a message (the message concept) before they can read one back. An educator who knows the list sees the thinking inside a page of repeated loops.

Emilia Ferreiro and Ana Teberosky, working with Spanish-speaking children in Argentina and Mexico, published Literacy Before Schooling in 1979 (English 1982). They found that children hold theories about what writing is and change them in a steady order. First, writing and drawing are the same, and then they separate. Next a child decides that a word needs at least a few marks and that the marks must vary. Then comes the idea that each mark stands for a syllable, then a mix of syllables and letters, and at last the alphabetic idea that letters stand for sounds. The syllable step shows more clearly in Spanish than in English. We read their work for what it says about children as theory-makers, and we never use it to place a child.

Anne Haas Dyson spent years in urban kindergarten and primary classes, and her books, including Writing Superheroes (1997), show that children's writing grows out of talk, drawing, play and the stories they love. A child writes to join a friend's game or to make a sign that works. Our reasons to write, the mailbox, the signs and the menus, come from her finding that writing starts social.

Judith Schickedanz, in Much More Than the ABCs (1999) and the later edition with Molly Collins (2013), followed children from scribbles through mock letters and letter strings to the first spellings, and found that a child's own name is usually the first word that matters and the first way in to letters. The Idea bank cards Writing center, Mail and letters and Bookmaking hold the set-ups that follow from all of this.

### The hand that writes

Colleen Schneck and Anne Henderson, occupational therapists, described in 1990 how grasp develops in children from three to six. A whole-hand hold with the arm doing the work (palmar grasp) gives way to fingers pointing down the tool (digital pronate grasp), then to thumb and two fingers with the hand still (static tripod grasp), and at last to thumb and two fingers moving on their own (dynamic tripod grasp), usually between four and six. The order is steady and the ages are wide. Crayons, chalk and pencils push back against the fingers, which is the science under our case against markers. Clay, dough, tongs, trowels and watering cans build the same hand.

Rhoda Kellogg, who sorted a million children's drawings, found that the twenty basic scribbles children make from about two, such as lines, loops, dots and zigzags, are the marks letters are later built from.

### Stages of writing by age

Our chart of fourteen stages is best read against our age bands. These are what many children show, with wide variation, and a child may move back and forth in a week.

- **Twos and threes.** Scribbles anywhere on the page, large and circular, with the whole arm. Toward three, marks get named after they are made, and a child may say "that says my name."
- **Threes and fours.** Scribbles move in lines (directional scribble), letter-like shapes appear, often from the child's name, and a child tells a story while drawing. The first letter of the name is often made on purpose.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Strings of letters, mostly capitals, then groups with spaces. The name written nearly right. Labels that match a first sound to a letter, words copied from the room, and reversals that are common and expected. Some children begin first and last sound spellings.
